### Model Adequacy Summary {#sec-generalized-poisson-gof-summary}

| **Check** | **GP model result** | **Same-split Poisson result** | **Verdict** |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Mean structure (observed vs fitted) | Correlation 0.38; scatter fans out with the fitted mean | Same mean trend available | Adequate as a width-only mean function; more regressors are assessable next |
| Dispersion test, $H_0: \theta = 0$ | LRT $= 80.48$, df $1$, $p = 2.9\times 10^{-19}$ | — | Strongly reject: the dispersion parameter is necessary |
| Pearson $\chi^2$ / df | 62.35 / 83 $= 0.75$; upper $p = 0.956$ | 252.70 / 84 $= 3.01$ | GP variance function adequate; Poisson's was three times too small |
| Residual deviance / df | 121.11 / 83 $= 1.46$ (nominal $p = 0.004$; approximation caveated) | 266.58 / 84 $= 3.17$ | GP halves the deviance; residual elevation partly artefactual at small counts |
| Zero-count check | 34 observed vs 27.4 expected | 34 observed vs 9.0 expected | GP recovers most of the zero shortfall; a surplus of about 7 zeros remains |

: Training-stage adequacy summary for the simple width-only Generalized Poisson model, contrasted with the same-split Classical Poisson fit. {#tbl-generalized-poisson-gof-summary .striped .hover}

**Decision.** The simple Generalized Poisson model repairs the two headline failures of the classical Poisson fit: the conditional variance is no longer three times too small, and the expected zero count is now at least of the right order of magnitude. Two cautions survive: a modest zero surplus (34 observed vs 27.4 expected) and the fingerprint that width alone is a thin mean model. Both motivate the next step of the workflow — adding the remaining phenotypic regressors, with the extended specification chosen to match @sec-classical-poisson-additional-regressors so that the comparison between the two chapters remains clean.

## Extending the Model with Additional Regressors {#sec-generalized-poisson-extended-model}

The goodness-of-fit audit of @sec-generalized-poisson-gof found the dispersion problem repaired but two items unresolved: a zero surplus the dispersion parameter cannot fully absorb (`r observed_zeros` observed versus `r round(expected_zeros_gp, 1)` expected zeros), and a thin one-regressor mean model. Following the workflow, we return to data modelling and fit the **extended specification** — the same four regressors as the extended model of @sec-classical-poisson-additional-regressors, with `Light` and `Both good` as reference categories:

$$
\log(\mu_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, \texttt{width\_cm}_i + \beta_2\, \texttt{weight\_kg}_i
+ \beta_3\, 1_{\{\texttt{Medium light}\}}(i)
+ \beta_4\, 1_{\{\texttt{Medium dark}\}}(i)
+ \beta_5\, 1_{\{\texttt{Dark}\}}(i)
+ \beta_6\, 1_{\{\texttt{One worn or broken}\}}(i)
+ \beta_7\, 1_{\{\texttt{Both worn or broken}\}}(i),
$${#eq-generalized-poisson-extended-model}

with the same GP random component $Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i \sim \operatorname{GPO}((1 - \theta)\mu_i, \theta)$. The dummy-variable arrangement is exactly the one tabulated in @tbl-classical-poisson-dummy-variable-arrangement of @sec-classical-poisson.

### Adding Phenotypic Regressors {#sec-generalized-poisson-phenotypic-regressors}

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-extended-fit-r
#| lst-cap: "Code to fit the extended Generalized Poisson model (width, weight, colour, spine condition) to the training data with VGAM."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Fitting the extended Generalized Poisson model
gp_fit_ext_r <- vglm(
  satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine,
  family = genpoisson1(zero = "dispind"),
  data = training_data
)

# Decoding the summary into a tidied coefficient table
cs_ext <- coef(summary(gp_fit_ext_r))
beta_rows <- c(
  "(Intercept):1", "width_cm", "weight_kg",
  "colorMedium light", "colorMedium dark", "colorDark",
  "spineOne worn or broken", "spineBoth worn or broken"
)
eta2_ext <- cs_ext["(Intercept):2", "Estimate"]
se_eta2_ext <- cs_ext["(Intercept):2", "Std. Error"]
theta_hat_ext <- 1 - exp(-exp(eta2_ext) / 2)
se_theta_ext <- (exp(-exp(eta2_ext) / 2) * exp(eta2_ext) / 2) * se_eta2_ext

gp_ext_summary_r <- tibble(
  Term = c(
    "(Intercept)", "width_cm", "weight_kg",
    "Colour: Medium light", "Colour: Medium dark", "Colour: Dark",
    "Spine: One worn or broken", "Spine: Both worn or broken",
    "Dispersion (theta)"
  ),
  Estimate = c(cs_ext[beta_rows, "Estimate"], theta_hat_ext),
  `Std. Error` = c(cs_ext[beta_rows, "Std. Error"], se_theta_ext),
  `z value` = Estimate / `Std. Error`,
  `Pr(>|z|)` = 2 * pnorm(-abs(`z value`))
)
```

:::

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-extended-fit-py
#| lst-cap: "Code to fit the extended model in Python; pd.get_dummies with drop_first=True reproduces R's treatment contrasts with the Light and Both good reference categories."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
```
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
# Building the extended design matrix with treatment-contrast dummies
cat_dummies = pd.get_dummies(training_data[["color", "spine"]], drop_first=True)
X_train_ext = np.column_stack(
    [
        np.ones(len(training_data)),
        training_data["width_cm"].to_numpy(dtype=float),
        training_data["weight_kg"].to_numpy(dtype=float),
        cat_dummies.to_numpy(dtype=float),
    ]
)

# Fitting the extended Generalized Poisson model
gp_fit_ext_py = GeneralizedPoisson(y_train, X_train_ext).fit_dispersion()
beta_hat_ext = gp_fit_ext_py.params[:-1]
beta_se_ext = gp_fit_ext_py.bse[:-1]
z_hat_ext = gp_fit_ext_py.params[-1]
theta_hat_ext_py = 2.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z_hat_ext)) - 1.0
se_theta_ext_py = (
    2.0
    * (1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z_hat_ext)))
    * (1.0 - 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z_hat_ext)))
    * gp_fit_ext_py.bse[-1]
)

# Tidied coefficient table
coef_names_ext = [
    "(Intercept)", "width_cm", "weight_kg",
    "Colour: Medium light", "Colour: Medium dark", "Colour: Dark",
    "Spine: One worn or broken", "Spine: Both worn or broken",
]
gp_ext_summary_py = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Term": coef_names_ext,
        "Estimate": beta_hat_ext,
        "Std. Error": beta_se_ext,
    }
)
gp_ext_summary_py["z value"] = (
    gp_ext_summary_py["Estimate"] / gp_ext_summary_py["Std. Error"]
)
gp_ext_summary_py["Pr(>|z|)"] = (
    2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(gp_ext_summary_py["z value"].abs()))
)
theta_row = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Term": ["Dispersion (theta)"],
        "Estimate": [theta_hat_ext_py],
        "Std. Error": [se_theta_ext_py],
        "z value": [theta_hat_ext_py / se_theta_ext_py],
        "Pr(>|z|)": [
            2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(theta_hat_ext_py / se_theta_ext_py)))
        ],
    }
)
gp_ext_summary_py = pd.concat([gp_ext_summary_py, theta_row], ignore_index=True)
gp_ext_summary_py_html = scrollable_table_html(gp_ext_summary_py)
```

:::

Both languages return a maximized log-likelihood of `r round(logLik(gp_fit_ext_r), 4)`, and the point estimates match to at least three decimals. The extended dispersion estimate is $\hat\theta = `r round(theta_hat_ext, 3)`$ (`Python`: `r round(reticulate::py$theta_hat_ext_py, 3)`), a variance-to-mean ratio of `r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2, 2)`: adding three sets of regressors barely moves the dispersion parameter (`r round(theta_hat, 3)` $\to$ `r round(theta_hat_ext, 3)`). The overdispersion in these data is **not** explained away by body size, colour, or spine condition — a likelihood-ratio test of $\theta = 0$ for the extended model gives $2 \times [`r round(logLik(gp_fit_ext_r), 2)` - (`r round(logLik(gp_poisson_ext_r), 2)`)] = `r round(lr_theta_ext, 2)`$ on one degree of freedom ($p \approx `r formatC(p_theta_ext, format = "e", digits = 1)`$).

### Did the Extension Pay Off? {#sec-generalized-poisson-nested}

The complementary question pits the two GP models against each other: does the four-regressor specification beat the width-only model? The nested likelihood-ratio statistic is

$$
2\,\big[\ell_{\text{extended}} - \ell_{\text{simple}}\big]
= 2 \times \big[`r round(logLik(gp_fit_ext_r), 2)` - (`r round(logLik(gp_fit_r), 2)`)\big]
= `r round(lr_nested_gp, 2)`,
$$

on $6$ degrees of freedom (eight coefficient columns against two), giving $p = `r round(p_nested_gp, 3)`$. Under the Generalized Poisson model the extra regressors do **not** jointly improve the training fit beyond what width already delivers.

The same-split Classical Poisson comparison — executed in the code above — tells a different story: there the nested statistic is `r round(lr_nested_poisson, 2)` on the same $6$ degrees of freedom, $p = `r round(p_nested_poisson, 3)`$. The point estimates barely moved between the two model classes; the **uncertainty** did. Because the Poisson model understates the variance, it overstates the evidence for the added regressors. This is the inferential argument for the GP model made concrete.

::: {.Tip}
:::: {.Tip-header}
Tip on keeping the extended specification anyway!
::::
:::: {.Tip-container}
Despite $p = `r round(p_nested_gp, 3)`$ on the nested test, the rest of this chapter continues with the extended specification, for two reasons. First, comparability: @sec-classical-poisson conducted its final assessment with this same regressor set, so holding the specification constant isolates the effect of the random component — the comparison this chapter exists to stage. Second, protocol discipline: the extended specification was fixed before model fitting as the set of available phenotypic variables (@tbl-generalized-poisson-study-design-variables), and the EDA supported a genuine colour gradient. The training-stage test results are reported exactly as they come out — both here and in the goodness-of-fit summary — rather than governing the specification post hoc.
::::
:::

### Goodness of Fit of the Extended Model {#sec-generalized-poisson-extended-gof}

The extended model passes through the same audit as the simple one; the executed numbers (computed in the listings above) are collected in @fig-generalized-poisson-extended-obs-fitted-r / @fig-generalized-poisson-extended-obs-fitted-py and in the summary below.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-extended-gof-r
#| lst-cap: "Code for the extended-model goodness-of-fit numbers (R)."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
mu_hat_ext <- as.numeric(fitted(gp_fit_ext_r)[, 1])
lambda_hat_ext <- (1 - theta_hat_ext) * mu_hat_ext
df_gof_ext <- nrow(training_data) - length(coef(gp_fit_ext_r))

# Pearson chi-squared with the GP variance function
pearson_ext <- sum((y_train_vec - mu_hat_ext)^2 / (mu_hat_ext / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2))
p_pearson_ext <- pchisq(pearson_ext, df = df_gof_ext, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Saturated-GP residual deviance
lambda_sat_ext <- vapply(
  y_train_vec,
  function(yi) {
    if (yi == 0) return(0)
    (yi * (1 - theta_hat_ext) + sqrt(yi^2 * (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2 + 4 * theta_hat_ext * yi)) / 2
  },
  numeric(1)
)
ll_sat_ext <- numeric(length(y_train_vec))
pos <- y_train_vec > 0
ll_sat_ext[pos] <- gp_logpmf_r(y_train_vec[pos], lambda_sat_ext[pos], theta_hat_ext)
ll_hat_ext <- gp_logpmf_r(y_train_vec, lambda_hat_ext, theta_hat_ext)
deviance_resids_ext <- sign(y_train_vec - mu_hat_ext) * sqrt(2 * (ll_sat_ext - ll_hat_ext))
residual_deviance_ext <- sum(deviance_resids_ext^2)
p_deviance_ext <- pchisq(residual_deviance_ext, df = df_gof_ext, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Zero-count expectation under the extended model
expected_zeros_ext <- sum(exp(-lambda_hat_ext))

cat(
  "Pearson:", round(pearson_ext, 2), "/", df_gof_ext,
  "=", round(pearson_ext / df_gof_ext, 2), "(upper p =", round(p_pearson_ext, 3), ")\n",
  "Deviance:", round(residual_deviance_ext, 2), "/", df_gof_ext,
  "=", round(residual_deviance_ext / df_gof_ext, 2), "(nominal p =", round(p_deviance_ext, 4), ")\n",
  "Expected zeros:", round(expected_zeros_ext, 1), "vs", observed_zeros, "observed\n"
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-extended-gof-py
#| lst-cap: "Code for the extended-model goodness-of-fit numbers (Python)."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
mu_hat_ext_py = np.exp(X_train_ext @ beta_hat_ext)
lambda_hat_ext_py = (1.0 - theta_hat_ext_py) * mu_hat_ext_py
df_gof_ext_py = len(y_train) - (X_train_ext.shape[1] + 1)

# Pearson chi-squared with the GP variance function
pearson_chisq_ext_py = float(
    np.sum((y_train - mu_hat_ext_py) ** 2 / (mu_hat_ext_py / (1 - theta_hat_ext_py) ** 2))
)
p_pearson_ext_py = stats.chi2.sf(pearson_chisq_ext_py, df=df_gof_ext_py)

# Saturated-GP residual deviance
lambda_sat_ext_py = np.zeros_like(y_train)
positive = y_train > 0
ys = y_train[positive]
lambda_sat_ext_py[positive] = (
    ys * (1 - theta_hat_ext_py)
    + np.sqrt(ys**2 * (1 - theta_hat_ext_py) ** 2 + 4 * theta_hat_ext_py * ys)
) / 2
ll_sat_ext_py = np.zeros_like(y_train)
ll_sat_ext_py[positive] = gp_logpmf(ys, lambda_sat_ext_py[positive], theta_hat_ext_py)
ll_hat_ext_py = gp_logpmf(y_train, lambda_hat_ext_py, theta_hat_ext_py)
deviance_resids_ext_py = np.sign(y_train - mu_hat_ext_py) * np.sqrt(
    2.0 * (ll_sat_ext_py - ll_hat_ext_py)
)
residual_deviance_ext_py = float(np.sum(deviance_resids_ext_py**2))
p_deviance_ext_py = stats.chi2.sf(residual_deviance_ext_py, df=df_gof_ext_py)

# Zero-count expectation under the extended model
expected_zeros_ext_py = float(np.sum(np.exp(-lambda_hat_ext_py)))

print(
    f"Pearson: {pearson_chisq_ext_py:.2f} / {df_gof_ext_py} = "
    f"{pearson_chisq_ext_py / df_gof_ext_py:.2f} (upper p = {p_pearson_ext_py:.3f})"
)
print(
    f"Deviance: {residual_deviance_ext_py:.2f} / {df_gof_ext_py} = "
    f"{residual_deviance_ext_py / df_gof_ext_py:.2f} (nominal p = {p_deviance_ext_py:.4f})"
)
print(f"Expected zeros: {expected_zeros_ext_py:.1f} vs {observed_zeros_py} observed")
```

The picture is consistent with the simple model's audit: the GP variance function remains adequate (Pearson ratio 0.89), the expected zero count creeps closer to the observed 34 but a surplus of about six remains, and $\hat\theta$ hardly budges. Whatever creates the extra zeros, it is not the omission of these regressors.

### The Inferential Payoff: Calibrated Standard Errors {#sec-generalized-poisson-se-comparison}

@tbl-generalized-poisson-se-comparison-r and @tbl-generalized-poisson-se-comparison-py put the extended GP fit side by side with the same-split, same-specification Poisson fit.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-se-comparison-r
#| lst-cap: "Code to compare Generalized Poisson and Poisson standard errors on the same specification and split (R)."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
gp_poisson_ext_r <- glm(
  satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine,
  family = poisson,
  data = training_data
)
cs_pois_ext <- coef(summary(gp_poisson_ext_r))

se_compare_r <- tibble(
  Term = c(
    "(Intercept)", "width_cm", "weight_kg",
    "Colour: Medium light", "Colour: Medium dark", "Colour: Dark",
    "Spine: One worn or broken", "Spine: Both worn or broken"
  ),
  `GP estimate` = cs_ext[beta_rows, "Estimate"],
  `GP SE` = cs_ext[beta_rows, "Std. Error"],
  `Poisson estimate` = cs_pois_ext[, "Estimate"],
  `Poisson SE` = cs_pois_ext[, "Std. Error"],
  `SE ratio` = `GP SE` / `Poisson SE`,
  `GP p-value` = 2 * pnorm(-abs(`GP estimate` / `GP SE`)),
  `Poisson p-value` = 2 * pnorm(-abs(`Poisson estimate` / `Poisson SE`))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-generalized-poisson-se-comparison-r
#| tbl-cap: "Generalized Poisson versus Poisson inferential comparisons on the extended specification (training data; R expected-information standard errors)."
#| message: false
print_as_dt(se_compare_r)
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-se-comparison-py
#| lst-cap: "Code to compare Generalized Poisson and Poisson standard errors on the same specification and split (Python)."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
poisson_ext_py = sm.GLM(y_train, X_train_ext, family=Poisson()).fit()

se_compare_py = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Term": coef_names_ext,
        "GP estimate": beta_hat_ext,
        "GP SE": beta_se_ext,
        "Poisson estimate": poisson_ext_py.params,
        "Poisson SE": poisson_ext_py.bse,
    }
)
se_compare_py["SE ratio"] = se_compare_py["GP SE"] / se_compare_py["Poisson SE"]
se_compare_py["GP p-value"] = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(
    (se_compare_py["GP estimate"] / se_compare_py["GP SE"]).abs()
))
se_compare_py["Poisson p-value"] = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(
    (se_compare_py["Poisson estimate"] / se_compare_py["Poisson SE"]).abs()
))
se_compare_py_html = scrollable_table_html(se_compare_py)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-generalized-poisson-se-comparison-py
#| tbl-cap: "Generalized Poisson versus Poisson inferential comparisons on the extended specification (training data; Python observed-information standard errors)."
#| message: false
#| results: asis
cat(
  "
",
  reticulate::py$se_compare_py_html,
  "
",
  sep = ""
)
```

Three observations carry the chapter's statistical message:

1. **The point estimates barely move.** The largest absolute change is on the intercept (`r round(cs_pois_ext[1, 1], 2)` $\to$ `r round(cs_ext["(Intercept):1", "Estimate"], 2)`); the regressor coefficients shift by at most a few hundredths. Generalizing the random component is not about changing the estimated associations.
2. **The standard errors inflate by 56% to 101%** (`SE ratio` column, `r round(min(se_compare_r$`SE ratio`), 2)` to `r round(max(se_compare_r$`SE ratio`), 2)`). The naive heuristic from equidispersion theory, a multiplicative $\sqrt{\text{Var}/\mathbb{E}} = \sqrt{`r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2, 2)`} = `r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_ext), 2)`$, is of the right order — the actual information-matrix inflation varies by coefficient because the Hessian geometry is not a flat rescaling.
3. **The inferential ranking of the regressors changes.** Under the Poisson model, `weight_kg`, `Colour: Dark`, and `Spine: Both worn or broken` all clear the conventional 5% line on this training split (p = 0.005, 0.010, 0.006); under the GP model none of them clearly does (p = 0.08–0.10, 0.04–0.07, and 0.08–0.09, varying slightly across the two information-matrix conventions). Chapter 10's own goodness-of-fit section documented that the Poisson model's variance was too small; the table above is the inferential price of that failure, made visible coefficient by coefficient.

The estimates themselves look reasonable; the *conclusions* are what changed. The next section reads the extended-model coefficients on their own merits, in the expected-count-ratio language of Chapter 10.

## Interpreting the Parameter Estimates {#sec-generalized-poisson-interpretation}

The extended fit of @sec-generalized-poisson-extended-model gives eight regression coefficients and one dispersion parameter. The coefficient interpretation follows Chapter 10's log-link logic exactly: on the log scale a coefficient changes the log expected count additively, so its exponential is a multiplicative **expected-count ratio**. What the Generalized Poisson layer changes is how much uncertainty we attach to those ratios — and, through $\theta$, how we describe the variability a given profile should expect.

### Interpreting the Continuous Regressors {#sec-generalized-poisson-continuous-regressors}

- **Shell width** ($\hat\beta_1 = `r round(cs_ext["width_cm", "Estimate"], 3)`$). Holding the other regressors fixed, a one-centimetre larger carapace is associated with an expected satellite count multiplied by $e^{\hat\beta_1} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["width_cm", "Estimate"]), 3)`$, a Wald 95% interval of (`r round(exp(cs_ext["width_cm", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_ext["width_cm", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_ext["width_cm", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_ext["width_cm", "Std. Error"]), 2)`) for that ratio. The point estimate is positive — larger crabs attract more satellites — but the interval includes $1$, so the training fit alone does not separate the width effect from zero once the other regressors share the credit.
- **Weight** ($\hat\beta_2 = `r round(cs_ext["weight_kg", "Estimate"], 3)`$). Holding the other regressors fixed, one additional kilogram is associated with an expected count multiplied by $e^{\hat\beta_2} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["weight_kg", "Estimate"]), 2)`$, with interval (`r round(exp(cs_ext["weight_kg", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_ext["weight_kg", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_ext["weight_kg", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_ext["weight_kg", "Std. Error"]), 2)`). One kilogram is a large step relative to the observed range (`r round(min(training_data$weight_kg), 1)`–`r round(max(training_data$weight_kg), 1)` kg), so it is also instructive to rescale: per 0.1 kg, the ratio is $e^{\hat\beta_2/10} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["weight_kg", "Estimate"] / 10), 3)`$.

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on interpreting width and weight together!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
In the training data the correlation between `width_cm` and `weight_kg` is `r round(cor(training_data$width_cm, training_data$weight_kg), 2)` — the two body-size measures largely carry the same information. "Holding the other fixed" is then a mathematical operation, not a description of a crab one is likely to see: a crab cannot easily gain a kilogram at fixed width. The individual width and weight intervals overlap substantially because the two regressors share their explanatory power; joint interpretation of the *size signal* (both coefficients positive, their linear combination tightly positive) is safer than strong claims about either coefficient on its own.
::::
:::

### Interpreting the Categorical Regressors {#sec-generalized-poisson-categorical-regressors}

For the categorical regressors, every coefficient is a contrast with the reference category (`Light` for colour, `Both good` for spine condition), so an exponentiated coefficient reads as the expected-count ratio *of the named category relative to its reference, other regressors held fixed*.

- **Colour.** Relative to a `Light` female of the same size and spine condition: `Medium light` $e^{\hat\beta_3} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["colorMedium light", "Estimate"]), 2)`$ (95% interval (`r round(exp(cs_ext["colorMedium light", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_ext["colorMedium light", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_ext["colorMedium light", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_ext["colorMedium light", "Std. Error"]), 2)`)), `Medium dark` $e^{\hat\beta_4} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["colorMedium dark", "Estimate"]), 2)`$ ((`r round(exp(cs_ext["colorMedium dark", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_ext["colorMedium dark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_ext["colorMedium dark", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_ext["colorMedium dark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`)), and `Dark` $e^{\hat\beta_5} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["colorDark", "Estimate"]), 2)`$ ((`r round(exp(cs_ext["colorDark", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_ext["colorDark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_ext["colorDark", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_ext["colorDark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`)). The estimates decrease monotonically: the point estimate for a `Dark` crab is about `r round(100 * (1 - exp(cs_ext["colorDark", "Estimate"])))`% **fewer** expected satellites than an otherwise identical `Light` crab, and its interval sits almost entirely below one. This direction matches the EDA gradient (@tbl-generalized-poisson-eda-categorical-r).
- **Spine condition.** Relative to `Both good`: `One worn or broken` $e^{\hat\beta_6} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["spineOne worn or broken", "Estimate"]), 2)`$ ((`r round(exp(cs_ext["spineOne worn or broken", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_ext["spineOne worn or broken", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_ext["spineOne worn or broken", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_ext["spineOne worn or broken", "Std. Error"]), 2)`)) and `Both worn or broken` $e^{\hat\beta_7} = `r round(exp(cs_ext["spineBoth worn or broken", "Estimate"]), 2)`$ ((`r round(exp(cs_ext["spineBoth worn or broken", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_ext["spineBoth worn or broken", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_ext["spineBoth worn or broken", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_ext["spineBoth worn or broken", "Std. Error"]), 2)`)). Both point estimates are above one, but both intervals comfortably include one; the small `One worn or broken` group (7 training crabs) has a particularly wide interval, as flagged in the EDA.

A results-sentence template for these fits, with placeholders filled from the training model: *"Among female crabs in the training data, and holding the other listed regressors fixed, [category] females had an estimated [ratio]-fold expected number of satellite males relative to [reference] females (95% Wald interval for the ratio: [lo]–[hi])."*

### Interpreting the Dispersion Parameter {#sec-generalized-poisson-theta-interpretation}

The dispersion parameter deserves interpretation of its own, because it is the reason this chapter exists. With $\hat\theta = `r round(theta_hat_ext, 3)`$, any crab profile with fitted expected count $\hat\mu_i$ carries

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(Y_i) = \frac{\hat\mu_i}{(1 - \hat\theta)^2} = `r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2, 2)`\,\hat\mu_i,
\qquad
\widehat{\operatorname{SD}}(Y_i) = \frac{\sqrt{\hat\mu_i}}{1 - \hat\theta} = `r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_ext), 2)`\,\sqrt{\hat\mu_i}.
$${#eq-generalized-poisson-theta-reading}

A concrete calibration makes the meaning tangible. For a profile with $\hat\mu_i = 3$: the GP model says counts fluctuate with variance `r round(3 / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2, 1)` (SD $`r round(sqrt(3 / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2), 1)`$), whereas a Poisson model with the same mean says variance $3$ (SD $`r round(sqrt(3), 2)`$). The GP model also implies $P(Y_i = 0) = \exp(-(1 - \hat\theta)\hat\mu_i) = `r round(exp(-(1 - theta_hat_ext) * 3), 3)`$ — versus `r round(exp(-3), 3)` under the Poisson model at the same mean. The dispersion parameter thus changes not only the widths of confidence intervals but the *shape* of every prediction this model makes: it more than quadruples the implied chance of an empty nest at this mean.

:::{.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Tip: reporting theta alongside the coefficients!
::::
::::{.Tip-container}
A one-line convention that travels well into reports and papers: **"fitted GP dispersion $\hat\theta = `r round(theta_hat_ext, 2)`$ (95% Wald interval `r round(theta_hat_ext - 1.96 * se_theta_ext, 2)` to `r round(theta_hat_ext + 1.96 * se_theta_ext, 2)`, implying a variance `r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2, 1)` times the mean."** Readers then see both the parameter and its consequence on a familiar scale. Reporting $\hat\theta$ alone is opaque; reporting only the ratio hides which side of the Poisson model the data landed on.
::::
:::

What changed relative to Chapter 10 is almost entirely *how sure we are*, not *which way the associations point*. Every statement above is still a training-stage statement: @sec-generalized-poisson-prediction turns to the predictive inquiry (held-out accuracy), and @sec-generalized-poisson-results will restate the inferential claims after refitting on the untouched testing set.

## Prediction with Generalized Poisson Regression {#sec-generalized-poisson-prediction}

Prediction proceeds exactly as in @sec-classical-poisson-prediction: form the linear predictor for a new profile, exponentiate to the expected-count scale, and — the GP addition — attach the fitted dispersion parameter. For a new female crab with regressor row vector $\mathbf{x}_{\operatorname{new}}^\top$ (intercept plus the seven extended-model regressors),

$$
\hat\mu_{\operatorname{new}} = \exp\big(\mathbf{x}_{\operatorname{new}}^\top \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\big),
\qquad
\hat\lambda_{\operatorname{new}} = (1 - \hat\theta)\,\hat\mu_{\operatorname{new}},
\qquad
Y_{\operatorname{new}} \mid \mathbf{x}_{\operatorname{new}} \sim \operatorname{GPO}\big(\hat\lambda_{\operatorname{new}}, \hat\theta\big).
$${#eq-generalized-poisson-prediction}

The predicted value $\hat\mu_{\operatorname{new}}$ is an **expected count**, not a rounded count: it can be fractional but must be positive. What the GP layer adds relative to Chapter 10 is an honest *predictive spread* — predictive SD $\sqrt{\hat\mu_{\operatorname{new}}/(1-\hat\theta)^2}$ — and it makes the whole satellite-count distribution available for the profile: its zero probability is $\exp(-\hat\lambda_{\operatorname{new}})$, its tail probabilities follow from the PMF, and so on.

### A Manual Prediction, First

Before delegating to software, walk through one prediction by hand. The first testing observation is a `Medium light`, `Both worn or broken` female of width `r testing_data$width_cm[1]` cm and weight `r testing_data$weight_kg[1]` kg (observed count: `r testing_data$satellites[1]`). Its linear predictor is

$$
\hat\eta = \underbrace{`r round(cs_ext["(Intercept):1", "Estimate"], 3)`}_{\hat\beta_0}
+ \underbrace{`r round(cs_ext["width_cm", "Estimate"], 4)`}_{\hat\beta_1}(`r testing_data$width_cm[1]`)
+ \underbrace{`r round(cs_ext["weight_kg", "Estimate"], 4)`}_{\hat\beta_2}(`r testing_data$weight_kg[1]`)
+ \underbrace{(`r round(cs_ext["colorMedium light", "Estimate"], 4)`)}_{\hat\beta_3}(1)
+ \underbrace{`r round(cs_ext["spineBoth worn or broken", "Estimate"], 4)`}_{\hat\beta_7}(1)
= `r round(sum(beta_hat_r1 <- c(cs_ext["(Intercept):1","Estimate"]) + cs_ext["width_cm","Estimate"] * testing_data$width_cm[1] + cs_ext["weight_kg","Estimate"] * testing_data$weight_kg[1] + cs_ext["colorMedium light","Estimate"] + cs_ext["spineBoth worn or broken","Estimate"]), 3)`,
$$

so $\hat\mu_1 = \exp(`r round(beta_hat_r1, 3)`) = `r round(exp(beta_hat_r1), 3)`$ and $\hat\lambda_1 = (1 - `r round(theta_hat_ext, 4)`) \times `r round(exp(beta_hat_r1), 3)` = `r round((1 - theta_hat_ext) * exp(beta_hat_r1), 3)`$. Under the fitted GP, $P(Y_1 = 0) = \exp(-\hat\lambda_1) = `r round(exp(-(1 - theta_hat_ext) * exp(beta_hat_r1)), 3)`$ — where a Poisson model with the same mean would say `r round(exp(-exp(beta_hat_r1)), 3)` — and the predictive standard deviation is $\sqrt{`r round(exp(beta_hat_r1), 2)` \times `r round(1/(1-theta_hat_ext)^2, 2)`} \approx `r round(sqrt(exp(beta_hat_r1) / (1 - theta_hat_ext)^2), 2)`$ rather than the Poisson $\sqrt{`r round(exp(beta_hat_r1), 2)`} \approx `r round(sqrt(exp(beta_hat_r1)), 2)`$. The software calls below reproduce exactly this arithmetic.

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on predicting with a dispersion parameter!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
A Poisson prediction collapses to its mean: once $\hat\mu_{\operatorname{new}}$ is computed, the whole predictive distribution is fixed. A GP prediction is a genuine two-parameter distribution: $\hat\mu_{\operatorname{new}}$ describes the *location* and $\hat\theta$ describes the *spread*. When $\hat\theta \approx 0.5$, the predictive SD is roughly $1/(1-\hat\theta) \approx `r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_ext), 2)`$ times the Poisson one at the same mean — so GP prediction intervals for individual counts are roughly twice as wide as the Poisson equivalents. Metrics that score the whole predictive distribution (the negative log predictive mass, the predictive deviance) will react to this honest widening; mean-only metrics (ME, MAE, RMSE) will not. Both families of metrics appear in @sec-generalized-poisson-results.
::::
:::

### Held-Out Predictions from the Training-Fitted Model

For the predictive inquiry, the rules of the workflow matter: **the extended model fitted on the training data is used to predict the testing observations**; no refitting happens before prediction. The tables below show the first ten held-out predictions and check explicitly that the manual linear-predictor arithmetic equals the software's fitted prediction.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-test-predictions-r
#| lst-cap: "Code to generate held-out expected-count predictions from the training-fitted extended GP model (R), including the manual-product check."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Design matrix for the testing data and the eight regression coefficients
mm_test <- model.matrix(~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine, data = testing_data)
beta_vec <- c(cs_ext["(Intercept):1", "Estimate"], cs_ext[beta_rows[-1], "Estimate"])
names(beta_vec) <- colnames(mm_test)  # renaming (Intercept):1 to (Intercept)
mu_test_r <- exp(drop(mm_test %*% beta_vec))

# The same predictions via VGAM's predict() method
mu_test_vglm <- predict(gp_fit_ext_r, newdata = testing_data, type = "response")
if (!is.null(dim(mu_test_vglm))) mu_test_vglm <- mu_test_vglm[, 1]
cat("Manual equals predict():", isTRUE(all.equal(mu_test_r, as.numeric(mu_test_vglm))), "\n")

# First ten testing predictions with predictive zero probabilities
gp_test_predictions_r <- testing_data |>
  mutate(
    predicted_expected_count = round(mu_test_r, 2),
    predictive_prob_zero = round(exp(-(1 - theta_hat_ext) * mu_test_r), 3)
  ) |>
  select(
    satellites, width_cm, weight_kg, color, spine,
    predicted_expected_count, predictive_prob_zero
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

## Results and Statistical Interpretation {#sec-generalized-poisson-results}

We now move from model building to results. Everything so far — EDA, both candidate GP fits, the dispersion tests, and all goodness-of-fit checks — ran on the training data. The testing set of `r nrow(testing_data)` crabs has not been touched since it was sealed in @sec-generalized-poisson-eda. The two guiding inquiries set out in @tbl-generalized-poisson-study-design-inquiries get separate answers:

| Inquiry type | Research question | What this results stage delivers |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **Inferential inquiry** | How is the expected number of satellite males associated with female crab width, weight, colour, and spine condition? | Coefficient-level inferential summaries from the extended Generalized Poisson model **refitted on the testing data**, including $\hat\theta$ with its uncertainty and the test of $H_0: \theta = 0$. |
| **Predictive inquiry** | How well can the available regressors be used to predict the expected number of satellite males for a female crab? | Held-out predictive metrics computed from the **training-fitted** extended model's predictions on the testing data, compared against a training-mean baseline. |

: The two guiding inquiries revisited for the Results section. {#tbl-generalized-poisson-results-inquiries .striped .hover}

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on why the testing data appear in two roles here!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
The two inquiries use the testing data differently, and the distinction matters:

- **Inferential**: the selected extended model is **refitted on the testing data**, giving a final coefficient-level analysis on observations never used for EDA, fitting, or goodness-of-fit decisions.
- **Predictive**: the model is **not** refitted; predictions for the testing responses come from the model fitted on the training data.

Mixing these roles would corrupt one branch or the other: the inferential refit is the workflow's guard against data-driven model selection, while held-out prediction is only meaningful before the model sees the testing responses.
::::
:::

### Inferential Results: Refitting on the Testing Data {#sec-generalized-poisson-inferential-results}

The extended specification of @eq-generalized-poisson-extended-model — same regressors, same reference categories, same GP random component — is refitted on the testing data with identical machinery:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-test-refit-r
#| lst-cap: "Code to refit the extended Generalized Poisson model on the testing data and assemble the inferential summary (R)."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Refitting the extended model on the testing data
gp_fit_test_r <- vglm(
  satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine,
  family = genpoisson1(zero = "dispind"),
  data = testing_data
)
poisson_test_r <- glm(
  satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine,
  family = poisson,
  data = testing_data
)

# Decoding the testing-refit summary
cs_test <- coef(summary(gp_fit_test_r))
eta2_test <- cs_test["(Intercept):2", "Estimate"]
se_eta2_test <- cs_test["(Intercept):2", "Std. Error"]
theta_hat_test <- 1 - exp(-exp(eta2_test) / 2)
se_theta_test <- (exp(-exp(eta2_test) / 2) * exp(eta2_test) / 2) * se_eta2_test

# Testing-set test of theta = 0
lr_theta_test <- 2 * (logLik(gp_fit_test_r) - logLik(poisson_test_r))
p_theta_test <- pchisq(lr_theta_test, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Coefficient table on the log expected-count scale
gp_test_summary_r <- tibble(
  Term = c(
    "(Intercept)", "width_cm", "weight_kg",
    "Colour: Medium light", "Colour: Medium dark", "Colour: Dark",
    "Spine: One worn or broken", "Spine: Both worn or broken",
    "Dispersion (theta)"
  ),
  Estimate = c(cs_test[beta_rows, "Estimate"], theta_hat_test),
  `Std. Error` = c(cs_test[beta_rows, "Std. Error"], se_theta_test),
  `z value` = Estimate / `Std. Error`,
  `Pr(>|z|)` = 2 * pnorm(-abs(`z value`)),
  `Ratio: exp(estimate)` = exp(Estimate),
  `Ratio 95% CI lower` = exp(Estimate - 1.96 * `Std. Error`),
  `Ratio 95% CI upper` = exp(Estimate + 1.96 * `Std. Error`)
)

# Exponentiated ratios are not meaningful for the dispersion parameter
gp_test_summary_r[
  gp_test_summary_r$Term == "Dispersion (theta)",
  c("Ratio: exp(estimate)", "Ratio 95% CI lower", "Ratio 95% CI upper")
] <- NA_real_
```

:::

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-test-refit-py
#| lst-cap: "Code to refit the extended Generalized Poisson model on the testing data and assemble the inferential summary (Python)."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
```
```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
y_test = testing_data["satellites"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

# Refitting the extended model on the testing data
gp_fit_test_py = GeneralizedPoisson(y_test, X_test).fit_dispersion()
poisson_test_py = sm.GLM(y_test, X_test, family=Poisson()).fit()
beta_hat_test = gp_fit_test_py.params[:-1]
beta_se_test = gp_fit_test_py.bse[:-1]
z_hat_test = gp_fit_test_py.params[-1]
theta_hat_test_py = 2.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z_hat_test)) - 1.0
s_z = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z_hat_test))
se_theta_test_py = 2.0 * s_z * (1.0 - s_z) * gp_fit_test_py.bse[-1]

# Testing-set test of theta = 0
lr_theta_test_py = 2.0 * (gp_fit_test_py.llf - poisson_test_py.llf)
p_theta_test_py = stats.chi2.sf(lr_theta_test_py, df=1)

# Coefficient table on the log expected-count scale
gp_test_summary_py = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Term": coef_names_ext,
        "Estimate": beta_hat_test,
        "Std. Error": beta_se_test,
    }
)
gp_test_summary_py["z value"] = (
    gp_test_summary_py["Estimate"] / gp_test_summary_py["Std. Error"]
)
gp_test_summary_py["Pr(>|z|)"] = (
    2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(gp_test_summary_py["z value"].abs()))
)
gp_test_summary_py["Ratio: exp(estimate)"] = np.exp(gp_test_summary_py["Estimate"])
gp_test_summary_py["Ratio 95% CI lower"] = np.exp(
    gp_test_summary_py["Estimate"] - 1.96 * gp_test_summary_py["Std. Error"]
)
gp_test_summary_py["Ratio 95% CI upper"] = np.exp(
    gp_test_summary_py["Estimate"] + 1.96 * gp_test_summary_py["Std. Error"]
)
theta_row_test = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Term": ["Dispersion (theta)"],
        "Estimate": [theta_hat_test_py],
        "Std. Error": [se_theta_test_py],
        "z value": [theta_hat_test_py / se_theta_test_py],
        "Pr(>|z|)": [
            2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(theta_hat_test_py / se_theta_test_py)))
        ],
        "Ratio: exp(estimate)": [np.nan],
        "Ratio 95% CI lower": [np.nan],
        "Ratio 95% CI upper": [np.nan],
    }
)
gp_test_summary_py = pd.concat([gp_test_summary_py, theta_row_test], ignore_index=True)
gp_test_summary_py_html = scrollable_table_html(gp_test_summary_py)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

#| message: false

:::

Reading the testing-set refit:

- **The dispersion parameter is a finding of the study, not a tuning detail.** The testing refit gives $\hat\theta = `r round(theta_hat_test, 3)`$ (95% Wald interval `r round(theta_hat_test - 1.96 * se_theta_test, 2)` to `r round(theta_hat_test + 1.96 * se_theta_test, 2)`), a variance `r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_test)^2, 1)` times the mean. The held-out likelihood-ratio test of $H_0: \theta = 0$ gives $\chi^2_1 = `r round(lr_theta_test, 2)`$, $p \approx `r formatC(p_theta_test, format = "e", digits = 1)`$: the equidispersion assumption fails on data the model never saw. Training and testing agree (compare $\hat\theta = `r round(theta_hat_ext, 3)`$ from @sec-generalized-poisson-extended-model), so the overdispersion is a stable feature of these crabs, not an artefact of one split.
- **One comparison keeps an interval below one: `Dark` vs `Light`.** Its testing estimate of `r round(exp(cs_test["colorDark", "Estimate"]), 2)` on the expected-count ratio scale has the 95% interval (`r round(exp(cs_test["colorDark", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_test["colorDark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`, `r round(exp(cs_test["colorDark", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_test["colorDark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`): an estimated `r round(100 * (1 - exp(cs_test["colorDark", "Estimate"])))`% lower expected satellite count for `Dark` females than for `Light` females of the same width, weight, and spine condition, with the interval just touching one. `Medium dark` points the same way (ratio `r round(exp(cs_test["colorMedium dark", "Estimate"]), 2)`, interval upper endpoint `r round(exp(cs_test["colorMedium dark", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_test["colorMedium dark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`).
- **Every other regressor interval comfortably contains one** on the testing refit — including both body-size measures, whose training-stage EDA gradient was the clearest signal in the chapter. Under the GP model's honest uncertainty, and with `r nrow(testing_data)` testing observations, the body-size association is not statistically distinguishable from zero in either half of the data once the remaining regressors are adjusted for (training width p = `r round(2 * pnorm(-abs(cs_ext["width_cm", "Estimate"] / cs_ext["width_cm", "Std. Error"])), 2)`; testing width p = `r round(2 * pnorm(-abs(cs_test["width_cm", "Estimate"] / cs_test["width_cm", "Std. Error"])), 2)`).

Overall inferential answer: *on the testing-set refit, female crab colour contrasts against `Light` — with `Dark` in particular — provide the clearest evidence of association with the expected number of satellite males, while the body-size effects do not clear the GP model's honest uncertainty bands; simultaneously, the dispersion parameter is decisively positive, so any final interpretation must use the GP model's standard errors rather than Poisson ones.*

### Predictive Results: Held-Out Metrics for the Training-Fitted Model {#sec-generalized-poisson-predictive-results}

For the predictive branch, we evaluate the predictions produced in @sec-generalized-poisson-prediction. @tbl-generalized-poisson-prediction-metric-guide lists the six metrics; they are the GP analogues of the six metrics of @tbl-classical-poisson-prediction-metric-guide in @sec-classical-poisson.

| Metric | Definition | Reading |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| Mean error (ME) | $\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} (y_i - \hat\mu_i)$ | Average signed error; near zero means little average bias, but signs can cancel. |
| Mean absolute error (MAE) | $\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} |y_i - \hat\mu_i|$ | Typical absolute error in counts. Smaller is better. |
| Root mean squared error (RMSE) | $\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} (y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2}$ | Penalizes large errors more than MAE. Smaller is better. |
| Mean GP deviance | $\frac{2}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{test}}}\big[\ell_i^{\text{sat}} - \ell_i\big]$ with $\ell_i = \log p_Y(y_i;\hat\lambda_i,\hat\theta)$ and $\ell_i^{\text{sat}}$ from @eq-generalized-poisson-saturated | Likelihood-based discrepancy of the fitted GP distribution with the saturated GP fit for each testing observation. Smaller is better. |
| Average KL discrepancy | Half of the mean GP deviance | The same evidence as the mean GP deviance on the KL scale (the two rows always move together). Smaller is better. |
| Mean negative log predictive mass | $-\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} \log p_Y(y_i;\hat\lambda_i,\hat\theta)$ | Average predictive surprise under the fitted GP distribution; this metric reacts to the *honest spread* that $\hat\theta$ provides. Smaller is better. |

: Prediction metrics used to evaluate held-out testing performance for the fitted Generalized Poisson model. {#tbl-generalized-poisson-prediction-metric-guide .striped .hover}


::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R` Code**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-generalized-poisson-test-metrics-r
#| lst-cap: "Code to compute the six held-out prediction metrics for the extended GP model and the intercept-only baseline (R)."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Intercept-only GP baseline fitted on the training data
gp_baseline_r <- vglm(
  satellites ~ 1, genpoisson1(zero = "dispind"), data = training_data
)
mu_baseline_r <- exp(coef(gp_baseline_r)["(Intercept):1"])
theta_hat_baseline <- 1 - exp(-exp(coef(gp_baseline_r)["(Intercept):2"]) / 2)

# Metric helper: all six metrics need only observed counts, fitted means, and theta
gp_prediction_metrics_r <- function(observed, mu_pred, theta_pred) {
  lam <- (1 - theta_pred) * mu_pred
  ll <- gp_logpmf_r(observed, lam, theta_pred)
  ll_sat <- vapply(
    observed,
    function(yi) {
      if (yi == 0) return(0)
      lam_sat <- (yi * (1 - theta_pred) + sqrt(yi^2 * (1 - theta_pred)^2 + 4 * theta_pred * yi)) / 2
      gp_logpmf_r(yi, lam_sat, theta_pred)
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
  dev <- 2 * (ll_sat - ll)
  c(
    `Mean error` = mean(observed - mu_pred),
    MAE = mean(abs(observed - mu_pred)),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean((observed - mu_pred)^2)),
    `Mean GP deviance` = mean(dev),
    `Average KL discrepancy` = mean(dev) / 2,
    `Mean negative log predictive mass` = mean(-ll)
  )
}

y_test_vec <- testing_data$satellites
gp_prediction_metrics_table_r <- round(rbind(
  `Extended GP model` = gp_prediction_metrics_r(y_test_vec, mu_test_r, theta_hat_ext),
  `Training-mean baseline` = gp_prediction_metrics_r(
    y_test_vec, rep(mu_baseline_r, length(y_test_vec)), theta_hat_baseline
  )
), 3)
```

gp_prediction_metrics_table_r |>

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
# Metric helper: all six metrics need only observed counts, fitted means, and theta
def gp_prediction_metrics(observed, mu_pred, theta_pred):
    lam = (1.0 - theta_pred) * mu_pred
    ll = gp_logpmf(observed, lam, theta_pred)
    ll_sat = np.zeros_like(observed)
    positive = observed > 0
    ys = observed[positive]
    lam_sat = (
        ys * (1 - theta_pred)
        + np.sqrt(ys**2 * (1 - theta_pred) ** 2 + 4 * theta_pred * ys)
    ) / 2
    ll_sat[positive] = gp_logpmf(ys, lam_sat, theta_pred)
    dev = 2.0 * (ll_sat - ll)
    return {
        "Mean error": float(np.mean(observed - mu_pred)),
        "MAE": float(np.mean(np.abs(observed - mu_pred))),
        "RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((observed - mu_pred) ** 2))),
        "Mean GP deviance": float(np.mean(dev)),
        "Average KL discrepancy": float(np.mean(dev) / 2),
        "Mean negative log predictive mass": float(np.mean(-ll)),
    }

# Intercept-only GP baseline fitted on the training data
gp_baseline_py = GeneralizedPoisson(y_train, np.ones((len(y_train), 1))).fit_dispersion()
mu_baseline_py = float(np.exp(gp_baseline_py.params[0]))
theta_hat_baseline_py = (
    2.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-gp_baseline_py.params[-1])) - 1.0
)

gp_prediction_metrics_table_py = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {"Model": "Extended GP model", **gp_prediction_metrics(y_test, mu_test_py, theta_hat_ext_py)},
        {
            "Model": "Training-mean baseline",
            **gp_prediction_metrics(
                y_test, np.full(len(y_test), mu_baseline_py), theta_hat_baseline_py
            ),
        },
    ]
).round(3)
gp_prediction_metrics_table_py_html = scrollable_table_html(gp_prediction_metrics_table_py)
```

If the regressors add out-of-sample predictive value, the extended model should beat this deliberately naive benchmark; if it does not, adding regressors has not bought prediction.

Reading the metric table honestly: the extended model and the baseline are close on every metric, and the ranking splits. On the absolute-error family the baseline is slightly better (MAE `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Extended GP model", "MAE"], 3)` vs `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Training-mean baseline", "MAE"], 3)`; RMSE `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Extended GP model", "RMSE"], 3)` vs `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Training-mean baseline", "RMSE"], 3)`); on the distribution-sensitive side the extended model wins the negative log predictive mass (`r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Extended GP model", "Mean negative log predictive mass"], 3)` vs `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Training-mean baseline", "Mean negative log predictive mass"], 3)`) while losing the mean GP deviance (`r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Extended GP model", "Mean GP deviance"], 3)` vs `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Training-mean baseline", "Mean GP deviance"], 3)`). The held-out correlation between observed and predicted counts is only `r round(cor(y_test_vec, mu_test_r), 2)`.

The predictive answer is therefore sobering: **the crab regressors do not buy reliable held-out point predictions beyond the training-mean benchmark on this split** — the same conclusion Chapter 10 reached for the Classical Poisson model, reproduced here under a better-calibrated distribution. What the GP model buys is not a lower MAE; it is *correctly sized uncertainty*: predictive distributions whose spread matches the data (so a predictive $\hat P(Y = 0)$ of `r round(exp(-(1 - theta_hat_ext) * mu_test_r[1]), 2)` is defensible where the Poisson `r round(exp(-mu_test_r[1]), 3)` was not) and inferential standard errors that survive refits.

| **Perspective** | **Deliverable** | **Conclusion for this case study** |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Point-prediction error | ME, MAE, RMSE | Extended model roughly ties or slightly trails the training-mean baseline; no regressor-driven predictive edge out of sample. |
| Distributional prediction error | Mean GP deviance, average KL discrepancy, mean negative log predictive mass | Mixed: NLPM favours the extended model, deviance favours the baseline; differences small either way. |
| Inferential calibration | Testing-refit Wald intervals; LRT of $\theta = 0$ | Dispersion decisively present ($\hat\theta \approx 0.51$, ratio $\approx 4.2$); `Dark`-vs-`Light` the clearest association; Poisson-standard-error conclusions would overstate the evidence. |

: Structure of the predictive and inferential results summary on the held-out testing data. {#tbl-generalized-poisson-results-summary .striped .hover}

## Storytelling {#sec-generalized-poisson-storytelling}

The **storytelling stage** translates the full Generalized Poisson workflow into a message for an applied audience. Imagine presenting to marine biologists studying horseshoe crab reproduction. They care about two distinct things, and the story keeps them separate:

- **Inferential**: which female characteristics are associated with the expected number of satellite males, and how certain are we?
- **Predictive**: do those characteristics help predict satellite counts for crabs we have not measured?

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-thread-needle-diy-sew-6230155/).](img/thread.png){width="350"}

The journey to the answer matters as much as the answer. Chapter 10's Classical Poisson model failed these data: the conditional variance was roughly three times the mean, expected zeros were less than a third of what was observed, and its residual deviance was far above its degrees of freedom. This chapter's candidate — Generalized Poisson regression — adds exactly one parameter aimed at exactly those failures. The training-stage audit showed the repair working: the Pearson statistic with the GP variance function is in line with its degrees of freedom, the expected zero count moved from `r round(expected_zeros_poisson, 1)` to `r round(expected_zeros_gp, 1)` (against `r observed_zeros` observed), and the likelihood-ratio test formalized the need for the dispersion parameter.

From the inferential point of view, the motivating question was:

> **How is the expected number of satellite males associated with female crab width, weight, colour, and spine condition?**

Two findings carry the answer. First, the **dispersion itself is a finding**: on the testing-set refit, $\hat\theta = `r round(theta_hat_test, 2)`$ per @tbl-generalized-poisson-test-refit-r, the counts vary about $`r round(1 / (1 - theta_hat_test)^2, 1)`$ times as much as a Poisson model with the same mean would allow, and the test of $H_0: \theta = 0$ is decisive ($p \approx `r formatC(p_theta_test, format = "e", digits = 1)`$). Any scientific statement about these crabs that ignores this dispersion is built on an unsound uncertainty floor.

Second, within the proper uncertainty the evidence concentrates on **colour**. Relative to `Light` females, `Dark` females are estimated to have `r round(100 * (1 - exp(cs_test["colorDark", "Estimate"])))`% fewer expected satellite males (95% interval for the ratio from `r round(exp(cs_test["colorDark", "Estimate"] - 1.96 * cs_test["colorDark", "Std. Error"]), 2)` to `r round(exp(cs_test["colorDark", "Estimate"] + 1.96 * cs_test["colorDark", "Std. Error"]), 2)`), and `Medium dark` points the same way with a wider interval. The body-size variables that dominate the raw plots do not carry a statistically decisive adjusted effect at this sample size — an honest disappointment that the GP model states plainly precisely *because* its standard errors are calibrated. Stakeholders should hear that sentence whole: *the association story is about colour; the size-gradient visible in exploratory plots is not, at these sample sizes, distinguishable from chance under a model whose uncertainty we trust.* Chapter 10's Poisson-based refit read slightly more generously [@sec-classical-poisson-storytelling]; the difference is not new data but correctly sized intervals.

From the predictive point of view, the motivating question was:

> **How well can the available regressors be used to predict the expected number of satellite males for a female crab?**

Plainly: the regressors are not reliable point predictors on held-out crabs. The extended GP model's held-out MAE is `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Extended GP model", "MAE"], 2)` satellites against `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Training-mean baseline", "MAE"], 2)` for a rule that always predicts the training average of `r round(mu_baseline_r, 2)`; RMSE tells the same story (`r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Extended GP model", "RMSE"], 2)` against `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Training-mean baseline", "RMSE"], 3)`). Only the distribution-aware negative log predictive mass tilts marginally toward the extended model (`r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Extended GP model", "Mean negative log predictive mass"], 3)` against `r round(gp_prediction_metrics_table_r["Training-mean baseline", "Mean negative log predictive mass"], 3)`), reflecting the better-calibrated spread rather than better locations.

The responsible story, then, is not "*the model explains satellite counts*". It is:

> *Satellite counts are strongly overdispersed — a stable, tested property of these data, present on data the model never saw. After adjusting honestly for this dispersion, the clearest association is darker colour with fewer satellites; the observed body-size gradient is compatible with a wide range of adjusted effects, including none. Used predictively, the crab characteristics give an honest picture of how uncertain any single crab's count remains, rather than an accurate point forecast.*

That is a usable scientific message, and it is only available because the model was allowed to say how variable the world is. The [Negative Binomial](#sec-negative-binomial) and [Zero-Inflated Poisson](#sec-zero-inflated-poisson) chapters show two alternative routes to overdispersion and zero surplus (variance *quadratic* in the mean; a two-component zero process); the exercises compare them directly against what was done here.

## Chapter Summary {#sec-chapter-13-summary}

This chapter presented **Generalized Poisson (GP) regression** as the book's answer to count data that violate equidispersion **in either direction**. The running horseshoe crab case study framed the two guiding inquiries summarized in @tbl-generalized-poisson-chapter-summary-inquiries.

| Inquiry type | Guiding question | Main takeaway |
|:---:|:---:|:---|
| **Inferential inquiry** | How is the expected number of satellite males associated with female crab width, weight, colour, and spine condition? | Dispersion is decisively present ($\hat\theta \approx 0.51$ on the testing refit, variance about $4.2\times$ the mean, $H_0: \theta = 0$ rejected overwhelmingly); the `Dark` vs `Light` colour contrast is the clearest adjusted association; body-size effects do not clear GP-calibrated uncertainty at this sample size. |
| **Predictive inquiry** | How well can the available regressors be used to predict the expected number of satellite males for a female crab? | Held-out point prediction does not beat a training-mean baseline (MAE 2.53 vs 2.50); the GP model's contribution is calibrated predictive spread, not lower error. |

: Summary of the two guiding inquiries in the Generalized Poisson regression case study. {#tbl-generalized-poisson-chapter-summary-inquiries .striped .hover}

The model itself has three parts (@sec-generalized-poisson-data-modelling): a **random component** $Y_i \mid \mathbf{x}_i \sim \operatorname{GPO}(\lambda_i, \theta)$ with mean $\mu_i = \lambda_i/(1-\theta)$ and variance $\mu_i / (1-\theta)^2$; the **systematic component** $\eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}$; and the **log link** $\log \mu_i = \eta_i$, which ties the rate-like parameter to the regressors through $\lambda_i = (1-\theta)\exp(\eta_i)$. The dispersion parameter $\theta \in (-1, 1)$ carries the meaning: $\theta = 0$ nests the Classical Poisson model as an *interior* point, $\theta > 0$ inflates the variance above the mean, and $\theta < 0$ compresses it below the mean. The Chapter 13 distributional summary in @sec-generalized-poisson-distribution collects the distribution's properties independently of any regression.

Estimation is **joint maximum likelihood** in $(\boldsymbol{\beta}, \theta)$ — there is no iteratively reweighted least squares shortcut as in a classical GLM — and uncertainty comes from the inverse information matrix, with the expected-versus-observed information difference explaining small `R`/`Python` discrepancies (@sec-generalized-poisson-estimation). In `R`, {VGAM}'s `vglm()` with `genpoisson1(zero = "dispind")` fits the model and we decoded its dispersion row back into $\theta$; in `Python`, the chapter's own `GenericLikelihoodModel` subclass maximizes the log-likelihood directly, with the logistic map keeping $\theta$ in $(-1, 1)$.

Goodness of fit ran as a full training-stage audit (@sec-generalized-poisson-gof): the likelihood-ratio test of $\theta = 0$ (classical $\chi^2_1$ applies because $0$ is interior), the Pearson statistic standardized by the GP variance function, the observed-versus-fitted comparison, the residual deviance with its small-counts approximation caveat, and the GP zero-count check $\sum_i \exp(-\hat\lambda_i)$ — the check that flagged the remaining zero surplus as the feature a dispersion parameter cannot repair on its own.

Interpretation kept Chapter 10's grammar (@sec-generalized-poisson-interpretation): coefficients are additive on the log expected-count scale and multiplicative as **expected-count ratios**, categorical coefficients compare against reference categories, and $\theta$ was given its own reporting convention (parameter plus its implied variance multiplier).

The results stage delivered the conclusions on held-out data (@sec-generalized-poisson-results): inference from a testing-set refit, prediction from the training-fitted model, six executed metrics against an intercept-only GP baseline, and an honest answer to both inquiries.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-confused-6230199/).](img/aha.png){width="300"}

Where does this model sit among the book's count-model tools? **Negative Binomial** regression (@sec-negative-binomial) models overdispersion with a variance quadratic in the mean, and **Zero-Inflated Poisson** regression (@sec-zero-inflated-poisson) models a structural zero surplus with a mixture; both are one-direction tools. The Generalized Poisson model's distinguishing feature is the sign of one scalar: it treats overdispersion and underdispersion symmetrically, which is why this book places it as the capstone of the mean-variance-flexible count models. The 99 B-Line coding case at the end of the chapter exercises the underdispersed side of the same machinery — where the Classical Poisson model errs in the *opposite* direction — and the practice exercises develop the conceptual material (the dispersion parameter's geometry, comparison with the sibling models, and the dispersion ratio as decision quantity).

## Case Study 2: 99 B-Line Bus Arrivals (Underdispersion) {#sec-cs2-bline}

We now turn to a setting where the count data exhibits the opposite problem. The 99 B-Line is the busiest bus route in Canada, running along Broadway from Commercial-Broadway SkyTrain station to the UBC Bus Loop. During weekday morning peak hours (7-9 AM), TransLink actively manages the headway between buses, targeting roughly 20 arrivals per hour at the UBC Bus Loop. Unlike the horseshoe crab dataset, where biological heterogeneity drove variance above the mean, the 99 B-Line's regulated schedule suppresses variance *below* what a Poisson process would predict, a natural underdispersion story.

We recorded the number of 99 B-Line buses arriving at the UBC Bus Loop per one-hour window across 200 weekday mornings. The predictors are day of week (Monday through Friday, with Monday as the reference category) and whether it was raining (0 = clear, 1 = raining). Rain introduces minor delays along the route but TransLink's headway management means arrivals remain more regular than random even in wet weather.

The sample mean of `buses_per_hour` is approximately 19.75 and the sample variance is approximately 13.90, giving a variance-to-mean ratio of 0.70. This is clearly below 1.0, the data is underdispersed.

### Data Collection and Wrangling {#sec-cs2-wrangling}

The dataset is loaded directly from `99_bline_arrivals.csv`. No train/test split is applied here since the primary goal of this case study is to demonstrate the underdispersion workflow and the interpretation of a negative $\hat{\delta}$, rather than predictive modelling.

### Goodness of Fit

We begin by fitting a Classical Poisson regression with `day_of_week` and `is_raining` as predictors, then test the equidispersion assumption using the same likelihood ratio test from the Goodness of Fit section above:

$$
\Lambda = -2\left(\ell_{\text{Poisson}} - \ell_{\text{GP}}\right) \sim \chi^2_1.
$$

For the 99 B-Line data, the Classical Poisson fit produces a residual deviance smaller than its degrees of freedom, the opposite pattern from the crabs dataset. The LR test confirms $\hat{\delta} < 0$ with a small $p$-value, establishing that underdispersion is present and that GP regression is warranted.

#### Interpreting the Dispersion Parameter

For the 99 B-Line data, $\hat{\delta} < 0$, reflecting the underdispersion we observed in the raw counts. The interpretation mirrors the crabs case but in the opposite direction:

- $\hat{\delta} < 0$ and the 95% CI excludes 0: underdispersion is confirmed; GP is preferred over Classical Poisson.
- The implied dispersion ratio $1/(1-\hat{\delta})^2 < 1$ tells us the variance is a fraction of the mean, counts cluster more tightly around their expected value than a Poisson process would allow.
- Practically: the 99 B-Line's active headway management compresses the distribution of hourly arrivals. TransLink is, in effect, fighting the randomness that would otherwise produce Poisson-like counts.
- Under underdispersion, Classical Poisson *overestimates* standard errors, making real associations harder to detect. Where the crabs analysis risked false positives, the bus analysis would risk false negatives if Classical Poisson were used instead.

#### Comparing Classical Poisson vs. Generalized Poisson

For underdispersed data, Classical Poisson overestimates standard errors. This means that predictors which are genuinely associated with hourly bus counts may appear non-significant when they should not. The GP model corrects this by accounting for the tighter-than-Poisson distribution of counts.

## Storytelling

This chapter introduced the Generalized Poisson distribution as a single, flexible framework for count regression when the equidispersion assumption of Classical Poisson fails, in either direction.

Our two case studies illustrate why this flexibility matters. In the horseshoe crab analysis, satellite counts varied dramatically from nest to nest: some females attracted many males, others attracted none, driven by real biological heterogeneity in shell size and condition. This heterogeneity pushes variance above the mean ($\hat{\delta} > 0$). Classical Poisson, blind to this extra variability, underestimated standard errors and would have led us to overstate the statistical significance of predictors like shell width and color. The GP model absorbed this extra variability into $\hat{\delta}$ and produced more honest, conservative inference.

In the 99 B-Line analysis, the story was structurally opposite. TransLink's active headway management meant that hourly bus arrivals were more predictable than random, counts clustered tightly around 20 per hour with less spread than a Poisson process would allow ($\hat{\delta} < 0$). Classical Poisson, assuming variance equals mean, would have overstated uncertainty and potentially missed real associations between day of week, weather, and arrival counts. The GP model again corrected the inference by estimating a negative $\hat{\delta}$ that captured the regularity in the data.

The practical lesson is that $\hat{\delta}$ is not just a nuisance parameter, it is a substantive description of the data-generating process. A positive $\hat{\delta}$ says the world is more heterogeneous than a simple Poisson model assumes. A negative $\hat{\delta}$ says the world is more regular. In either case, ignoring it leads to unreliable inference. The GP model makes that structure explicit and measurable.
